text: The Subcommittee on Early Childhood, Elementary, and Secondary Education will come to order. I note that a quorum is present. Without objection, the chair is authorized to call recess. At any time. The notion that every student should go to college was perhaps well-intended, but it was never compatible with the needs of young people or of our country. While every student should have the opportunity to go to college, this is not the only path to success. Thankfully, in recent years, we've seen a renewed commitment to supporting alternate pathways, in particular career and technical education. While CTE is not new, its value has often been overlooked or dismissed in recent decades as the fallback option for students who don't fit into the traditional academic mold. Today, there is no denying its critical role in preparing the workforce for a skills-forward economy. CTE is for students who want to build, create, and lead. It is for students who learn best by doing. Over 8 million secondary school students nationwide are already participating in CTE programs. They're learning to design, weld, code, and provide life-saving care. These students gain hands-on experience that leads to good and stable jobs. And the results speak for themselves. Students who concentrate in CTE, completing more than 2 credits, graduate at rates above 90%, significantly higher than the national average. CTE participation also boosts academic achievement and even promotes college readiness in itself. More than 40 states allow students to take CTE courses through dual enrollment programs at technical or community colleges, enabling them to earn college credits in high school. This can lead to associate's degrees, bachelor's degrees, and industry-recognized credentials. And students are eager for these opportunities. 85% of recent high school graduates took at least one CTE course. CTE classrooms are filled with future engineers, healthcare professionals, business owners, and innovators. It's not a second option. It's a pathway to success in high school, higher education, and the workforce. How we prepare our students today will determine not just their future success, but our nation's economic strength. Job creators across the country are struggling to find workers who have the right skills. This present and growing gap threatens our nation's economic competitiveness. Employers are looking for candidates who demonstrate skills, not just degrees, to meet the demands of an economy with 7.2 million open jobs. In our dynamically changing economy, we must reimagine student programs to meet the demands of today's and tomorrow's labor market. And that's what CTE is all about. By design, it equips students with skills that match real job opportunities, providing pathways to immediate employment. That means fewer unfilled jobs, more career-ready graduates, and a stronger economy. I look forward to hearing from our witnesses who have built exceptional career and technical education programs and to discussing how we can strengthen and expand their work at schools across America. With that, I'll turn to the ranking member for an opening statement.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, and thank you to the witnesses. We've been I know we've both been looking forward to this hearing. I appreciate this hearing today where we can talk about the importance of career and technical education, which historically has had bipartisan support. But I do want to address the recent deeply troubling actions that threaten the effectiveness of CTE and longstanding bipartisan legacy. Earlier this year, President Trump kicked off his second term by signing an executive order to dismantle and close the Department of Education. As part of that effort, the executive branch used a questionable interagency agreement, an IAA, to transfer much of the administration of CTE and adult education programs from the Department of Education to the Department of Labor. Along with this, $2 billion in funding for programs under the Office of Career and Technical Education was transferred out of the Education Department to the Department of Labor. Just yesterday, the department announced six new interagency agreements to move more critical education programs to the Departments of Labor, Interior, Health and Human Services. This is not routine. The consequences of this agreement will be far-reaching. It's also part of a broader effort to shut down the Department of Education without the consent of Congress. We should all be concerned about the destructive message of shutting down the Department of Education. What does that say about our country? Scattering programs and resources across offices that aren't equipped to administer them will hurt students and schools. And I want to make clear today that we must fight to reclaim our Article I responsibility and conduct oversight over the administration to reverse this irresponsible decision. Moving the administration of CTE to the Department of Labor is a mistake for many reasons. First, CTE is more than job training or short-term job placement. It helps students, many of them as early as middle school, explore careers, build skills, and prepare for higher education or long-term careers in high-demand fields. That kind of lifelong learning pipeline can't be built or maintained without staff who have spent their careers crafting educational pathways, not just administering workforce training grants, which is also important, but a different task. Offloading these programs to an agency that lacks that background is a disservice to our children, to the future. And it also violates the Perkins Act, which I worked with several of my colleagues here today to reauthorize in 2018 when it was signed into law by President Trump. Second, these programs are objectively worse off now that they've been moved to the Department of Labor. Under the Department of Education, the programs were aligned with academic standards, focused on long-term success, and embedded into the education ecosystem at the state and local level. The Department of Labor's job training programs, by contrast, are often short-term, disconnected from education systems, and focused on immediate employment rather than sustained learning. This shift risks turning CTE into the type of narrow vocational training we worked for decades to move away from. We support it, but not it's not the same as CTE, where students, often from low-income families or communities of color, were tracked into limited job paths with little room for upward mobility. Ironically, the transfer of these programs from Education to the Department of Labor has created more bureaucratic inefficiencies, not reduced them. States, school districts, and institutes of higher education are now forced to navigate two different agencies to access one program. We've heard stories from states who are spending all their time learning a new grant management system instead of doing what they should be doing, which is innovating. Delays in grant processing and decision-making are already being reported, and we've only begun to see the fallout. It's pretty chaotic. And third, the innovation we've seen in CTE over the past decade is now at risk. And that progress was made possible because states had the flexibility to tailor programs to meet the needs of their students and local economies. But this new hyperpartisan shift, driven not by educational best practices, but by ideology, threatens to stifle innovation. A bipartisan success story is now being drawn into a federal bureaucratic tug-of-war, placing unnecessary hurdles in front of states that were leading the way in expanding access and improving outcomes, including my home state of Oregon. I want to emphasize, career and technical education works. It works because it's education-driven. It works because it was crafted in a bipartisan manner and in partnership with educators, employers, and communities. And it works because it's the kind of engaging, hands-on, problem-solving learning that engages students. And it works because we had career professionals in the Department of Education who understood the difference between preparing students for the future and just placing them in a job. I wish we could spend the whole hearing discussing the exciting innovations in CTE that states like my home state of Oregon are leading. My state's made CTE a priority. We've seen absenteeism decrease. We've seen graduation rates increase. I've toured amazing programs, including a culinary arts program at Lincoln High School in Portland, a fish hatchery management program at Warrenton High School on the coast, health sciences in Hillsboro, and a program in Sherwood, Oregon, where students actually design, build, and then sell a home. These have provided incredible opportunities for students to learn collaboration, critical thinking, communication, responsibility. But unfortunately, this administration is dragging us into another partisan fight. Just look at the Heritage Foundation's Project 2025, which laid the groundwork for this illegal move of moving the program and shutting down the Department of Education. So we can't afford to let CTE be undermined. Congress must reject this transfer, restore the programs at the Department of Education where they belong, and guarantee that any future changes go through the proper legislative channels, not through backdoor bureaucratic maneuvers. Our goal should be to improve and innovate CTE. This isn't just a matter of process. It's protecting learning for millions of learners. And I do, Mr. Chairman, as I yield back, want to introduce a few pieces for the record about some of the work that Oregon has done. There's a report from Stand for Children on how Oregon's Measure 98, which prioritized career and technical education, resulted in significant growth in student achievement and graduation rates; second, a piece from the Oregon Capital Chronicle celebrating the 97.7% high school graduation rate of students enrolled in two or more CTE classes last year in 2024; and an article from the Portland Business Journal on how Portland Community College is investing in CTE and partnering with industry to develop high-quality course offerings. So thank you, Mr. Chairman. I look forward to the witnesses' testimony, and with that, I yield back.

Pursuant to Committee Rule 8(c), all members who wish to insert written statements into the record may do so by submitting them to the committee clerk electronically in Microsoft Word format by 5:00 p.m. 14 days after this hearing. And without objection, the hearing record will remain open for 14 days to allow such statements and other extraneous material noted during the hearing to be submitted for the official hearing record. I know that some of our colleagues who are not permanent members of this subcommittee may be joining us at today's hearing. I'll now introduce our witnesses. Our first witness is Dr. Deb Volzer, the Vice President for Workforce Development at SME in Worthington, Ohio. Our second witness is Mrs. Kristi Rice, a cybersecurity teacher at Spotsylvania High School in Spotsylvania, Virginia. Our third witness is Mr. Braden Goetz, a senior policy advisor at the Center on Education & Labor at New America here in Washington, D.C. And our fourth witness is Mrs. Nicole Gasper, the CEO of the West Michigan Aviation Academy in Grand Rapids, Michigan. We thank the witnesses for being here today, and we look forward to your testimony. Pursuant to committee rules, I would ask that you each limit your oral presentation to a 3-minute summary of your written statement. As committee members have many questions for you, the clock will count down from 3 minutes. However, pursuant to Committee Rule 8(d) and committee practice, we will not cut off your testimony until you reach the 5-minute mark. I would also like to remind the witnesses to be aware of their responsibility to provide accurate information to the subcommittee. I will first recognize Dr. Volzer for your testimony.

Thank you, Chairman Kiley and Ranking Member Bonamici, and distinguished members of the committee. I truly thank you for the opportunity to speak on this critical issue today. I'm representing SME, the national nonprofit with nearly 100 years of experience in building manufacturing talent and accelerating advanced technology adoption. We have trained millions of incumbent workers, inspired hundreds of thousands of students, and work daily with employers, educators, workforce agencies, and community partners across our country, from small businesses to Fortune 500s. What truly sets SME apart is our dual perspective. We are not only at the table shaping national strategy, we are inside the four walls of industry every single day. This connection gives us real-time insight into what manufacturers need now and how to deliver scalable, high-impact training solutions that meet our manufacturers' needs. Our manufacturers are giving us a stark warning: their workforce is aging, their skills gap is widening, and too few young people are entering the manufacturing workforce. This is the reality facing our country, and the stakes could not be higher. We are not facing a future workforce problem; we are facing a future workforce crisis. And while investing in K-12 is essential, it's simply not enough. As such, we urge Congress and state leaders to expand access to modern, industry-connected CTE programs in every community to equip the next generation for high-wage, high-tech manufacturing careers. SME's Education Foundation PRIME program is active in over 118 high schools across 25 states, and through a four-year pathway, students gain hands-on experience working with industrial equipment and software, leading to the acquisition of industry-relevant skills. We support this pipeline with teacher training, sustainability funding, and award over $1 million annually in scholarships. The strength of SME's education and training relies on our direct industry engagement. We know firsthand that when this vital connection is not there, it weakens or breaks down, students risk learning outdated skills on outdated equipment with outdated processes that no longer meet the evolving demands of modern manufacturing. SME's PRIME program is solving this issue at scale. And while SME PRIME and other programs can train the next generation of talent, we cannot overlook one of the most underrecognized challenges in workforce development: the shortage of qualified instructors. Without instructors, programs stall, learners wait, skill development slows, and our nation's manufacturing capabilities weaken. SME is actively addressing this challenge through our Maritime Manufacturing Workforce Pipeline. This program is designed to meet critical shipbuilding needs across the Gulf Coast and INDOPACOM regions, and by integrating K-12 and postsecondary pathways in alignment to industry competencies in a cohesive K-20 model, we are building short, mid, and long-term solutions to support both current and future workforce demands. And finally, I would be remiss if I did not clearly state that technology is transforming manufacturing at an unprecedented pace, from automation and data analytics to advanced robotics and artificial intelligence. To keep up, our workforce and training programs need continuous alignment, requiring deep industry engagement. In closing, as mentioned, the stakes have never been higher, and we are facing a defining moment for U.S. manufacturing. A strong, skilled, and future-ready workforce is not just an economic asset; it is a strategic necessity. Thank you for the opportunity to speak on this critical issue, and please know that SME will continue to innovate, collaborate, and lead the adoption of technology while building talent to leverage that technology to preserve our global manufacturing might. I look forward to your questions.
Thank you very much. Mrs. Rice, you're now recognized for your testimony.

Good afternoon, Chairman Kiley and Ranking Member Bonamici and members of the committee. Thank you for the opportunity to speak today. My name is Kristi Rice, and I teach cybersecurity at Spotsylvania High School, a rural high school in Spotsylvania, Virginia. Despite our rural setting, we have built one of the most dynamic and successful cybersecurity programs in the Commonwealth, if not the nation. I teach a three-level pathway and coach the award-winning Cyber Knights. In my classroom, I like to think outside the box. Instead of only lecturing about threats and defenses, my students learn through hands-on, gamified activities like capture the flag competitions. They solve real-world challenges in cryptography, forensics, and network defense. As a coach for the U.S. Cyber Team, I bring back elite-level strategies from international competition and adapt them for high school students, showing them that cybersecurity is not just a class, but a pathway to national service and high-demand careers. I also push my students to get outside the box, literally. My students have toured the Pentagon, visited FBI headquarters, presented at the White House Quad Cyber Challenge, and attended cybersecurity conferences and networking events. For many of our rural students, these are the first experiences that help them see themselves as future professionals protecting critical systems and infrastructure. Some of these students are here today. To expand access, I founded the Virginia High School Cyber Cup, a hands-on cybersecurity competition hosted by the Virginia and U.S. Cyber Range Cloud CTF platform. I also co-founded the Cyber Circuit. It's a virtual cybersecurity club that includes students whose schools don't yet offer cybersecurity or who are homeschooled. These efforts ensure that any student anywhere in Virginia can step into the cybersecurity world. Innovation in CTE must also support our educators. Through the GenCyber Teacher Program with Virginia Tech and the University of North Georgia, I help prepare new teachers to teach cybersecurity in their first year. And in my role as a Career Kickstart facilitator and pilot teacher for the College Board's AP Cybersecurity course, I support educators nationwide on building a high-quality pathway. The impact is clear. Six of my former students have earned the DOD SMART Scholarship. Many now work with federal agencies and in industry. A high percentage of my students graduate with the CompTIA Security+, and we have seen a strong increase in female participation. What's at stake is our national security and our economic future. If we don't connect classroom to career in fields like cybersecurity, we risk falling behind in both talent and readiness. When we invest in educators, empower our students, and create pathways that connect classroom to real-world challenges, we don't just prepare students for jobs, we prepare them to protect and lead in the digital frontier. Thank you for your time today.
Thank you very much. Mr. Goetz, you're recognized for your testimony.

Good afternoon, Chairman Kiley, Ranking Member Bonamici, and members of the subcommittee. I appreciate the opportunity to testify. As you mentioned, I'm a senior policy advisor in the Center on Education & Labor at New America. My written testimony highlights some CTE innovations and talks about some recommendations for Perkins reauthorization. But I think the best use of my time is to first thank you for your past support of CTE, and then to appeal to you to help us return Perkins to the Department of Education. Before New America, I worked for 26 years for the Department of Education, most of that time in the Office of Career, Technical, and Adult Education, or OCTAE. When I joined Ed, CTE, then known as vocational education, was not well-regarded. It was on the margins of public education, an undemanding alternative that taught a narrow set of skills for specific jobs that were, many of which were low-wage. Since that time, CTE leaders and policymakers like yourselves have transformed vocational education. It is now CTE now prepares students with durable skills for college and career. The transfer of Perkins to the Department of Labor threatens that progress. Operationally, it is a muddle because Perkins Perkins is very clear that the Secretary of Education is the only one who can make policy decisions. What Ed has done is transferred the implementation of her decisions to DOL. So, they sent over a team of OCTAE employees who report to a DOL career official, who report to a policymaking official, who, on up through the chain of command, to the Secretary of Labor. I don't understand how the work gets done. When Secretary McMahon makes a decision, does she call the Secretary of Labor and ask her to communicate that down the chain? And what happens if the OCTAE employees at the bottom of the chain have questions or they have other other issues they need policy decisions on? Do they communicate that back up the chain and the two secretaries talk? It's also confusing and inefficient. DOL also does not have expertise in Ed regulations, like charter school funding. North Dakota just passed a new charter school law. They're going to be coming to the Department of Labor asking for help in understanding Ed's regulations for charter schools. Good luck to them. Also troubling are the implications for ensuring that all students have equal access and opportunities to succeed in CTE. Since 1979, state Perkins agencies have been responsible for proactive civil rights monitoring. It's also known as Methods of Administration. The department has not clarified what happened to those responsibilities and who's helping them with them. And some states have been struggling to get access to their money. Yesterday, I was surprised to hear the department put out a fact sheet that said that 35 grantees had accessed their Perkins money since the transfer. Well, there are more than 35 Perkins grantees and it's been 2 months. It's been very difficult for states. There are 57 grantees, including D.C., Puerto Rico, outlying areas, Virgin Islands, but only 35 have access. And for all of this, from what I understand, Ed is paying DOL $200,000 per quarter. That's a lot of money to pay for something you can do yourself. Of course, you could address all of these problems and simply amend Perkins and move it to DOL, but that would be a mistake. CTE is fundamentally an education program. It is not job training. DOL's training programs serve an important function by helping adults who are out of work find work quickly. The most common programs are in ground transportation, like truck driving, and nursing occupations that require less than an associate's degree. Many of them pay less than the median wage. That is not the orientation or the result we want for high school CTE programs. We need to be building long-term pathways to prosperous futures for every student, not steering them into the next available job regardless of its quality. Moving Perkins also puts DOL— puts the federal government out of step with the states. CTE is universally regarded as a CTE program by states. 47 states and the District of Columbia run Perkins out of a K-12 agency or higher ed agency. Locating Perkins at DOL threatens to remarginalize CTE. We have made so much progress. Please do not let Secretary McMahon take us back. Thank you.
Thank you very much, and Mrs. Gasper, you're recognized for your testimony.

Chairman Kiley and Ranking Member Bonamici and members of the committee, thank you so much for the opportunity to share with you what we get to do with and for our families at the West Michigan Aviation Academy. We are a public charter high school located at the Gerald R. Ford International Airport in Grand Rapids, Michigan, where we get the privilege of serving just over 600 students in grades 9 through 12. We are heavily focused on aviation, as our name indicates, but also heavy STEM, and the piece that really sets us apart is our professional culture. At the academy, career and tech ed is key to what we get to do for our young people. It's critical to our mission. We get to create meaningful talent pipelines. And over the 15 years, we've demonstrated that by having just under 200 high school seniors earn their private pilot's licenses by the time they've graduated. We've also had 27 of our students earn their Part 107 commercial drone licenses. Both of them are portable credentials that our young people get to walk out of our high school with. Our robotics team has found themselves multiple times on the world stage down in Texas, and we've also had a state-recognized Science Olympiad team. Our students currently in our Build-A-Plane course, we've not only built a Carbon Cub EX-2 that was deemed airworthy, that we sold to replenish the project, but now our students are refurbishing a 1975 Bellanca Scout and a 2-33 Schweizer glider, both of which are real-world skills. Additionally, to give you a picture of our school, we have 6% of our graduates, on average, choosing military service. So, while that's not specifically CTE, it does show an additional pathway, and that is three times the national average of young people graduating going into the military. These accomplishments address our workforce needs. We know the global demand in the aviation sector is great. We're looking at a need of over 600,000 pilots and technicians over the next decade and additionally 15,000 over the next couple of years for the domestic pilot shortage. Our mission, vision, and values guide every decision we make at the academy, and we believe that excellence truly begins with both connection and upholding high expectations. Every student is paired with a trusted adult where we get to uphold clear and high standards. For example, we don't issue D's. Our students get to earn A, B, C, or F. Our students get to earn 26 credits to graduate for their high school diploma, where the state of Michigan requires 18. Our students also get the opportunity to give 100 hours of community service as part of their diploma from the academy, along with a required job-shadowing opportunity. Because we're located at an airport, you can imagine the unique opportunities that get to come our way. We believe that students need a lot of exposure during their formative years, and so that is a key element of our academy. Students have access to our direct flight line. We also have access to the airport public safety, and we have an incredible amount of guests that get to visit our students to share different career opportunities within the aviation and engineering sectors. We've even had students test for landmines with a partner at the airport as well. However, these partnerships extend beyond the airport. We have our wonderful charter authorizer, Grand Valley State University, who also, along with other postsecondaries, give our students dual credit for the CTE programs in which they participate. All of our aviation programs are state-certified in CTE. Additionally, we've also taken the lead in the state of Michigan in working with other partners to help develop the CTE standards for aviation general and professional pilot programs. I'm very proud to say that 66% of our juniors and seniors are involved in CTE at our academy. My hope today is that I can share the West Michigan Aviation Academy with you as a national model that can show what is possible when you have business and industry, private partnerships, and public education coming together for the central mission of serving our young people. It truly does create a pathway to career for our young people as they get to experience all that's in front of them. Again, thank you so much for the opportunity. I look forward to your questions.

Thank you very much. Under Committee Rule 9, we'll now question witnesses under the 5-minute rule, and I'll first recognize myself for 5 minutes. And I just want to thank all our witnesses. Really inspiring testimony. I think a big part of what we do on this subcommittee, apart from the policy levers we have, is to showcase just truly tremendous examples of what's going on at school districts across the country. And as Mrs. Gasper just said, what you're doing, what all of you are doing really provides a national model that I hope can be a source of inspiration in, in every state. So I do want to just briefly address off the top this issue of the interagency agreements and the Perkins program. And so, Mr. Goetz, you raised a number of criticisms of this, and the ranking member as well, and I don't want to dismiss that. I want to really try to understand it. I think there's probably room for debate whether the chain of authority that you described is exactly as you described it. Certainly, if there are issues accessing the grants, that's something that needs to get worked out quickly. But as far as sort of your broader critique, the problem, as you describe it, seems to be that, well, DOL is going to have to talk to the Education Department, then they're going to have to call each other back and forth. But kind of the entire premise of CTE programs is we want to have this connection and coordination between schools and in industry, right? So, so what's wrong with sort of recapitulating that or mirroring that in terms of fostering greater coordination between the Department of Education and DOL? Well, I think in

past administrations we've had a lot of close coordination between the two departments, including in Mr. Trump's first term. They met constantly, and we were often collaborating on issues where we intersect. Registered apprenticeship is an example of that. In Mr. Trump's first term, the department put out a guide to aligning CTE with apprenticeship. In Mr. Biden's term, we put out a memo about registered apprenticeship being an allowable use of Perkins funds. So we have had that collaboration and cooperation. We don't need to do it through an interagency agreement where we transfer the entire program over to another another agency.

All right. Well, thank you, Dr. Volzer. Thank you very much for your testimony. And The point you made that I think is really important is just the way things are changing so fast in the workplace right now when it comes to AI and robotics and everything else, that you need to sort of have that perspective like in real time in order to have your programs really be serving the needs of our workforce. I guess the challenge is that because things are changing so rapidly, what students learn in CTE programs may quickly, you know, become not applicable to the workforce. As it exists 1, 2, 3, 5 years from now. Now, they'll be gaining additional skills once they're in the workforce. But that seems to me like the fundamental challenge is how do we structure these programs in an era where we know that students, once they graduate from them, are going to be in a rapidly evolving workforce?

Thank you for your question. And I think that really is where it comes down to deep integration with local industry and alignment to education. Not only how the programs are designed, but making sure that the skills that are being taught in those classrooms are directly applicable inside the four walls of industry. One of the things that the SME PRIME program does specifically is we do a a significant amount of research into the industries, the equipment that's being used, the processes that are being used, the new technologies that are being integrated, and make sure that that same exact equipment is inside the walls of the high school so that when they step into that, they are productive day one. They are continuing to learn, and in fact, they're bringing innovation. That is what the next generation of learners— it's not just about the technical skills, it's not just about the academic skills, it's not just about those workplace-ready skills. It's the innovation that the next generation is bringing because they are comfortable with technologies. And that is what is inspiring the next adoption of technologies inside our our classrooms. And so I would say, to me, this is while you look at national systemic issues of— and we really have to pay attention to our small- to medium-sized manufacturers. They often can't step outside their four walls to really engage with academic education leaders. We have to make sure that we're reaching inside those four walls so that we can align and make sure there is that continuous education and skill-ready development.

Very well said. Thank you. And I guess that sort of capacity to adapt and innovate within a particular domain is itself sort of the core skill set in many cases that you're trying to teach. Mrs. Rice, just very quickly, I was very excited to read your and hear your testimony. I know that we've had big shortages when it comes to cybersecurity, and so I wanted to just ask a little bit more about the pathway, because I think a lot of people think that, well, cybersecurity is just kind of an offshoot of software engineering or some other field. Not true at all, right? So, what is sort of the distinct nature of your pathway and the needs that it fills?

My pathway, cybersecurity, there's a huge skills gap, and there's currently over 600,000 jobs that are open right now across the nation. And personally, in my pathway in Virginia, we have a three-course pathway including we have an intro class, we have a networking class, and then we have a more advanced class. And it gets the kids prepared for the Security+ and the Net+.
Thank you very much. I'll now recognize the ranking member.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and thank you to the witnesses. Wonderful testimony, all of you. Appreciate it. And I want to follow up on the chairman's question about the pace of change. Mr. Goetz, you said in your written testimony that job training is not CTE, and CTE is not job training. In fact, you cited an article from 1986 in which experts recommended abandoning rote, entry-level job training and reforming what was then called vocational education, as you explained, to integrate academics, teach teamwork, critical thinking skills. And here's a quote from your testimony: "prepare young people for a working life of continual learning, problem solving, and communicating." And I couldn't agree more. And I submit that's even more critical today than it was in 1986. With the pace of change, things are very different than they were in 1986. There were no computers in classrooms in 1986, students didn't have cell phones, we didn't have AI. It's a different world. And preparing students for the jobs of the future is not the same because we don't know what the jobs of the future will look like. It's very different. And CTE is important and beneficial because, as I mentioned, it's typically this hands-on, project-based learning. And when you look at the 21st-century job skills—collaboration, critical thinking, communication, confidence, creativity—those are skills that matter no matter what path someone takes, or no matter what job someone goes into. So we need to strengthen this and realize why CTE is important, and it's not what this administration is doing. They're kind of stuck, I think, back in 1986 when it's 2025. So, Mr. Goetz, the statutory requirements for Perkins program include academic achievement measures, alignment with postsecondary programs of study, support services that are embedded in educational institutions, and then transitions between secondary and postsecondary education. These are all elements that presume administration in an education-focused agency, as you mentioned. So is it correct that 77% of states implement CTE through their state education agency—that's K-12—14% through postsecondary education, and 6% through standalone CTE agencies?
That's correct.
sound right? So will those state entities be better served by the Department of Education or by the Department of Labor?
by the Department of Education, with whom they've had a relationship for many years.

and and the staff at the Department of Education who were accustomed to this work. And and also, Mr. Goetz, we've heard reports that the transfer of funding and administration has already caused some serious problems, as you mentioned. At least four states have reported they could not access Perkins formula grant funding during the transition period when OCTAE attempted to move grantees from Education's payment to the DOL's payment management system. And some states have reported delays in receiving their payee account numbers needed to access their formula Perkins funding, and other states have had challenges getting bank accounts to even be recognized by the new payment system. Other requirements like wet signatures, all these things are creating significant challenges in accessing formula dollars since the transition was initiated. And all of this suggests the transition from the Department of Education to the Department of Labor has failed. So could all of this have been avoided if the Perkins formula grants were still administered by the Department of Education?
Absolutely. They've made it harder to get Perkins funds than it is to get a mortgage.

And I want to emphasize, too, that this committee has worked hard on the Workforce Innovation Opportunity Act and other workforce programs. And those are important. I'm not minimizing those, but they're not the same as educational programs, such as the CTE programs that are mentioned. And we heard some great examples today. I think they're wonderful. There are so many industry partnerships that are happening. But again, the focus needs to be on career and technical education. It's not career and technical job training. And it's even more critical with CTE at middle schools and high schools. Again, we don't know what the jobs will look like. So Dr. Volzer, Mrs. Rice, and Ms. Gasper, do you agree with Mr. Goetz that career and technical education is education? Anybody disagree with that? Go ahead. Anybody Do you all agree that it is an educational program, career and technical education, is more of an educational program than a job training program? Go ahead, Dr. Volzer. I know this because I am an educator, if you can't tell already, but a person who has a cybersecurity background could not educate your students in the way that you did, in the way that you do, could not align that work to the standards, could not make sure that they're exploring and having a club and different opportunities. Ms. Gasper, you talked about many of your students, the percentage that go on to the military. In my school, every student enrolled in a Perkins program also took the ASVAB test, the practice test and the actual test, and their guidance counselors aligned them with the classes to make sure that if they didn't pass it the first time, they would pass it on their subsequent attempts. All of those things happen in schools. And there should be conversation and collaboration between business and the workplace, but teaching is a profession, and it is different. And just because someone runs a business doesn't mean that they can teach young people to love a career or have opportunities to explore, to fail and try again. So, I have a lot of questions, but I already know the answer to many of these questions, so a lot of this is rhetorical for me. What we should be doing on this committee is finding ways to match teachers with partners in the business world so that they can bring that real-life experience in real time to keep them updated. But we would be hard-pressed to think that someone who runs a successful business could stand in front of a classroom of high school students and transfer that knowledge and allow those kids to grasp that information. So, Ms. Rice, I really appreciate what you said about you don't care where the money comes from, you just want to make sure it's there and available for kids. But I hope you hold firmly to the last part of CTE, and that is the education part, and our kids deserve that aspect. My time is up. I have no questions.

Thank you. Thank you very much to the witnesses. I think it's been an excellent discussion, and I don't think there's any question that we all agree on the importance of career and technical education. That is clear. There is a difference in looking at career and technical education as education or looking at it as job training. I think we need to continue that conversation. I also want to note the full committee chairman, Mr. Walberg, talked about complimented Oregon, which I appreciate very much, and I just want to note that Oregon runs its CTE programs through our Higher Education Coordinating Commission that works with the Department of Education. Our workforce programs are run apprenticeships are run through our Bureau of Labor & Industries. But workforce and career and technical education are education. And I know from listening to the testimony today, especially Mr. Goetz, with your years of experience at the Department of Education, that the decision to transfer career and technical education programs from the Department of Education to the Department of Labor was not made with students or educators or communities in mind. It's part of a political agenda of eliminating the Department of Education. And that to me is incredibly disappointing when the people with expertise are losing their jobs and the expertise is not there anymore. What was once a cohesive education-rooted system designed to support lifelong learning is now being fractured between these two agencies, one that the administration wants to eliminate, and the two agencies have different missions and different capabilities. And as I said in my opening statement, CTE is not simply about job training or placement. It's about building pathways for students from middle school through postsecondary education and teaching them skills they can take into meaningful careers. And that work demands experienced educators and robust academic alignment. Deep coordination with local communities is something that the Department of Education has long provided. We're already seeing the consequences: delayed grants, disjointed program administration, the erosion of trust from those on the ground trying to implement the programs. And I do want to note as well that Perkins doesn't set curriculum. That is done at the local level. There's a suggestion that Perkins or the federal government is setting curriculum. We don't do that. That is up to the states and localities. And I think you could see by the testimony today that it is local decision-making. The Perkins dollars help. They help with equipment. They help with the funding. And let's not forget the broader context that this move is part of this, as I said, the strategy to dismantle the Department of Education, and that's part of the Heritage Foundation's Project 2025, is deeply concerning. This is not about job numbers or job training. If we care about student opportunity, if we care about educating students of today to fill all of the jobs of tomorrow, we cannot allow this misguided transfer to stand. We should restore these programs at the Department of Education and require that future changes go through Congress, not through political back channels. So, Mr. Chairman, I sincerely hope that we can work together to strengthen CTE programs, but especially I hope we can work together to counter this unprecedented power grab by the executive branch. This is not a decision that the executive branch can make on its own, but it's trying to. Congress needs to have a say. And I hope we can continue to talk about the harmful effects that dismantling the Department of Education will have on today's children and future generations. So I again appreciate all of your testimony and the great work that you're doing, and I look forward to further conversations. And I yield back the balance of my time.

Thank you very much to our witnesses. I think this has been a great hearing. It's been really inspiring to learn more about the incredible work that you're doing and the exciting educational opportunities you're providing for young people that put them on a path to fulfilling careers and provide a tremendous asset to our country. And thanks as well to the young people who are here as tremendous models. I look forward to meeting you guys here after the hearing, and thanks for coming to D.C. I also want to thank the members of the committee on both sides. While we are not always in total and complete harmony on every aspect of education policy, I am really encouraged that there is a substantial bipartisan support for CTE. I think that for a while the pendulum swung way too far towards this mantra of college for all, but now it's starting to swing back. We have tremendous momentum for CTE across the country, and we need to do everything we can here to keep that going. It's more important than ever now.
